newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers to face renewed EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers to face renewed EMU jitters.

text.p: Faced with growing uncertainty over a timely start to monetary union, European Union finance ministers will be under intense pressure to put the single currency back on a solid footing when they meet in Luxembourg on Sunday.

The gathering, which spills over into Monday, will be a critical test of the willingness of political heavyweights Germany and France to maintain their commitment to the euro currency's 1999 launch date, diplomats say.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, battered after a dispute with the country's powerful central bank over a revaluation of its gold assets, attends in a much weakened political state, both domestically and within the EU.

The ill-fated gold strategy was a desperate attempt to shore up Bonn's deteriorating finances and has left many analysts wondering whether Germany will be able to comply with its own strict rules in meeting the Maastricht treaty's entry criteria for economic and monetary union..

In France the lurch to the political left has prompted a fresh bout of uncertainty over the new government's commitment to the EU's stability and growth pact, a mechanism designed to enforce spending discipline among EMU members.

French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has said he did not feel bound by the pact, which includes stiff fines for governments with excessive deficits, and would seek a renegotiation of its stringent terms.
Jospin, attending a European Social Democratic Parties' Congress in Sweden, said Friday it was too soon to give his government's position on monetary union or the stability pact.
A Dutch diplomat, speaking for the current EU presidency in Brussels, said it had not received a formal request from France to reopen negotiations on the pact.

The prospect of renewed talks has been played down by EU officials, many of whom see the Socialist pre-election rhetoric shifting to a more centrist and European stance with the government now in office.
"An electoral campaign in France is one thing. The European realities are another," commented one EU diplomat.
The stability pact is expected to be nodded through by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 and then later ratified by EU finance ministers.
Diplomats say France's desire to see monetary union start on schedule should prevent a scenario in which the 15-nation bloc reconsiders pact, which was painstakingly put together.

For EMU's broader future, the developments in France and Germany have led financial markets to consider two very distinct options -- delay or a timely launch with a large number of countries, the so-called soft euro.
The latter scenario would necessitate a more flexible reading of the Maastricht criteria and thereby allow countries like Italy a better chance of entering EMU in 1999.

For Germany, this would mark an important political shift. Up to now, Bonn has argued for a strict interpretation of the criteria in order to assure a sceptical German public that the euro would be as strong as the mark.
Although Bonn appears to have lost the moral high ground in this debate, it is by no means clear how Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition will ultimately respond to a weak euro.
The fault lines have already begun to emerge, with Heiner Geissler, deputy floor leader in parliament for Kohl's Christian Democrats, calling Friday for a looser reading of the criteria.
Meanwhile, a leading German newspaper said that members of Waigel's CSU were discussing a possible delay due to the left-wing election victory in France.
The CSU is the Bavarian sister party of Kohl's CDU, the leading party in the ruling coalition that also includes the Free Democrats.

Waigel was forced to deny the embarrassing report, which said CSU state government and CSU members of the state assembly in Bavaria believed a single currency would be a "monetary death sentence" after France's Jospin suggested it could be launched with softer financial criteria.
